# Talking Villagers

A server-side Fabric mod that gives Minecraft villagers names, personalities, families and
politics — and lets you actually talk to them, in your own words, using a language model you run
yourself.

**Nothing is sent to any external service.** Speech is generated by [Ollama](https://ollama.com)
on your own machine. If Ollama is slow or missing, villagers simply go quiet; the server never
blocks waiting on it.

- **Minecraft** 26.3
- **Loader** Fabric ≥ 0.19.5, Fabric API, Java 25
- **Version** 2.1.0

## Vanilla clients can join

The mod is server-side only. Everything you see is expressed through mechanisms a vanilla client
already understands — entity names, Text Display entities, particles, titles, the action bar,
written books and chat. Install it on the server (or in singleplayer) and other players need
nothing.

There is one consequence worth knowing: because singleplayer runs an integrated server inside the
client, `fabric.mod.json` declares `"environment": "*"`. Do not change this to `"server"` — that
means *physical dedicated server only*, and the mod would silently stop loading in singleplayer.

## Setting up Ollama

1. Install Ollama from <https://ollama.com/download> (Linux: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`).
2. Pull a model. A 3B model is what this mod is tuned for:
   ```
   ollama pull llama3.2:3b
   ```
   The `model` setting in the config must match a name from `ollama list` exactly, including the
   tag after the colon.
3. Make sure Ollama is running — it usually starts with your computer and listens on port 11434.
   Otherwise `ollama serve`. Check with `curl http://localhost:11434`; a working server answers
   `Ollama is running`.
4. If Ollama is on the **same** machine as the Minecraft server, the default `base_url` already
   works.
5. If it is on a **different** machine, set `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` on that machine, restart Ollama,
   allow port 11434 through its firewall, and point `base_url` at its address.

The server log says whether Ollama could be reached. Villager replies render as floating text
above their heads, so they never appear in the client log — to confirm the model is answering, read
Ollama's own log.

## How to play

The mod adds **no commands at all**. Everything happens by playing.

| Do this | Get this |
|---|---|
| **Sneak + right-click a villager** (empty hand) | Start a conversation. Type normally — your chat goes to them, not to the server |
| **Sneak + right-click a villager holding a book** | A written *Villager Autobiography*: who they are, family, and everyone they know sorted by how they feel about them |
| **Sneak + right-click a village bell holding a book** | A written *Village Directory*: population, trades, food, mood, recent events and complaints |
| **Walk into a village** | A title with the village's name and how many live there |
| Say *bye*, walk more than `max_distance` away, or stay quiet 30 s | The conversation ends |

While a villager is composing an answer, `Nils is thinking…` floats over their head until the
reply arrives. Thinking models may reason first (`ollama.thinking`), which makes replies more in
character at the cost of a short wait.

Both books work with a plain `minecraft:book` or with one the mod already wrote (which rewrites it,
so a record is never stuck stale). Books are snapshots — they do not update on their own.

### Village politics

A settlement forms around a bell once villagers live there, and elects one of its own as mayor.
Reading the **sitting mayor's** book while standing in the village offers you `[Take over as mayor]`;
taking the office removes that button from your copy of the book. As mayor, the Village Directory
gives you `[Rename village]`, which asks for the new name in chat.

Those two buttons are the mod's only interactive controls. They use a vanilla `custom` click event,
so there is no command for anyone to type or forge — but the server still re-checks your standing
every time one is tapped.

### What villagers do on their own

- **Identity** — a name, gender (with a small chance of being transgender), an orientation, and one
  of the 16 MBTI types, which shapes how they speak and how often they start conversations.
- **Relationships** — a −100…+100 meter per person, moved by trading, gifts, being hit, watching a
  neighbour be killed, and by how kindly you spoke to them. It feeds vanilla trade prices, so being
  liked genuinely makes trading cheaper. A villager who hates you enough refuses to trade at all.
- **Talking to each other** — pairs chat periodically, and the outcome nudges both their opinions
  either way.
- **Gossip** — the village generates a handful of topics a day that residents bring up.
- **Families** — courtship, engagement, weddings (with fireworks), births, and grief when someone
  dies.
- **Jobs, homes and food** — villagers want a workstation and a bed, and farms have to feed the
  population. Unmet needs become complaints, and complaints that persist cost the mayor standing —
  including you, if you are the mayor.

## Configuration

Written to `config/talkingvillagers.toml` on first run, with comments explaining every setting.
Delete the file to regenerate it. Anything missing from your copy falls back to the shipped
default, so the file is safe to trim.

| Section | Settings |
|---|---|
| `[names]` | The name pools — male and female first names, surnames, and settlement name prefixes/suffixes. Ships with Swedish names |
| `[ollama]` | `base_url`, `model`, `thinking`, `timeout_ms`, `max_tokens`, `temperature`, `queue_capacity`, `health_check_interval_ticks`, `relationship_cap` |
| `[sexuality]` | `enable_sexuality` — false makes every villager heterosexual |
| `[conversation]` | `display` (`overhead` / `chat` / `both`), `overhead_duration_ticks`, `max_distance`, `particles_while_talking` |
| `[needs]` | `food_enabled` — whether settlements have to feed themselves |

Everything else that shapes village behaviour is fixed in `Tuning.java`, deliberately not exposed:
those are balance decisions, not deployment settings.

## Building

```
./gradlew build
```

The mod jar lands in `build/libs/talkingvillagers-1.0.0.jar`. Ignore the `-sources` jar.

To run a development client:

```
./gradlew runClient
```

No EULA is needed for that — that only gates `runServer`.

## Notes for contributors

Minecraft 26.2 dropped Yarn mappings, and 26.3 keeps it that way, so this builds against **Mojang
official mappings** and `build.gradle` has no `mappings` line. Writing villager or entity code from
1.20/1.21 memory produces code that does not compile, or worse, compiles and fails at runtime.

`docs/mc-26.2-api-notes.md` records every API difference already found the hard way, plus the 26.3
deltas found during the port — read it before
writing new code, and add to it rather than re-deriving. Ground truth comes from `./gradlew
genSources`, which puts decompiled sources under
`.gradle/loom-cache/minecraftMaven/net/minecraft/`.
